note.explanation: Plants can reproduce without seeds by using spores or vegetative parts, and sexually by producing gametes in flowers. In flowering plants, pollen carries the male gametes and the ovule contains the female gametophyte. Fertilization forms a seed, which can grow into a new sporophyte plant.
examples: A potato tuber can grow into a new potato plant.
A pollen tube carries male gametes to the embryo sac in an ovule.
note.checkAnswer: The pollen grain is the male gametophyte; the embryo sac is the female gametophyte.
note.simple: A plant can make a new plant from a plant part, or make seeds after fertilization. Flowers help make the male and female cells needed for seed formation.
note.checkQuestion: Which structure carries the male gametes from a pollen grain towards the embryo sac?
note.title: Reproduction in Plants: Main Ideas
steps: Identify whether reproduction is asexual or sexual.
For asexual reproduction, look for one parent and no fusion of gametes.
For sexual reproduction in flowering plants, follow pollen to the ovule.
Remember that fertilization forms the embryo and endosperm, and the ovule develops into a seed.
note.answer: The pollen tube carries the male gametes towards the embryo sac.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following organisms commonly reproduce by binary fission?
rationales: Yeast commonly reproduces by budding, not binary fission.
Bacteria commonly reproduce by binary fission.
Rhizopus reproduces by spores, not binary fission.
Plants reproduce by several methods, but binary fission is not their common method.

mcqs.stem: What is the primary method of reproduction in yeast?
rationales: Binary fission is not the primary method in yeast.
Spore formation occurs in some fungi, but yeast primarily reproduces by budding.
Budding is the primary method of reproduction in yeast.
Fragmentation is not the primary method in yeast.

options: They produce spores during sexual reproduction
They produce two kinds of spores
Spores can only grow into new fungi in dry environments
Spores are produced to withstand harsh conditions
mcqs.stem: Which of the following statements is true about spore formation in fungi?
rationales: Fungi commonly form spores asexually; this statement is not generally true.
The statement is not the key general fact about fungal spores in this question.
Spores do not only grow in dry environments; suitable conditions are needed for germination.
Spores can survive harsh conditions and are produced as a means of survival.

options: Creation of a bud that detaches from the cell
Splitting the cell into two identical daughter cells
mcqs.stem: What happens in some bacteria during harsh conditions?
rationales: Budding is not the survival response described for some bacteria.
Some bacteria form thick-walled endospores that help them survive harsh conditions.
Splitting into daughter cells is binary fission, not the response to harsh conditions asked for.
Fusion of bacterial cells is not the response described.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following is an example of vegetative propagation through runners?
rationales: Potato propagates through tubers.
Strawberry plants can propagate through runners.
Onion propagates through bulbs.
Ginger propagates through rhizomes.
Onion propagates through a bulb.
Potato propagates through tubers.
Ginger propagates through rhizomes.
Garlic propagates through a bulb.

mcqs.stem: The horizontal aboveground stem, which produces leaves and roots at its nodes;
rationales: A stolon is a horizontal aboveground stem that can produce roots and shoots at its nodes.
A bulb is an underground storage structure with fleshy leaves.
A rhizome is a horizontal underground stem.
A corm is a short, swollen underground stem.

mcqs.stem: Which of these does NOT help a plant for vegetative propagation?
rationales: A rhizome can produce new plants vegetatively.
A corm can produce new plants vegetatively.
A runner can produce new plants vegetatively.
A flower is involved in sexual reproduction, not vegetative propagation.

mcqs.stem: Which part of the flower is responsible for producing pollen?
rationales: The stigma receives pollen.
The anther produces pollen.
The ovary contains ovules.
The petal helps attract pollinators.

mcqs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a part of carpel?
rationales: The filament is part of the stamen, not the carpel.
The style is a part of the carpel.
The stigma is a part of the carpel.
The ovary is a part of the carpel.

mcqs.stem: Which structure forms the female gametophyte in flowering plants?
rationales: The pollen grain is the male gametophyte.
The female gametophyte, or embryo sac, develops within the ovule.
The anther produces pollen grains.
A sepal protects the flower bud and does not form the female gametophyte.

mcqs.stem: The male gametophyte in flowering plants is known as:
rationales: The pollen grain is the male gametophyte.
The embryo sac is the female gametophyte.
The ovary contains ovules; it is not the male gametophyte.
The carpel is the female reproductive organ of the flower.

mcqs.stem: In the life cycle of flowering plants, which structure is triploid (3n)?
rationales: The egg is haploid (n).
The fusion nucleus formed from the polar nuclei and one male gamete is triploid, but the named endosperm nucleus is the triploid structure among these choices in the textbook's terminology.
The endosperm nucleus is triploid (3n), formed after fusion with a male gamete.
A sperm is haploid (n).
The filament supports the anther and does not contain the embryo sac.
The anther produces pollen grains.
The style connects the stigma and ovary.
The embryo sac develops inside the ovule.

options: Fertilization of the egg by two male gametes
Fertilization of two eggs in the same embryo sac by two sperms
Fertilization of the egg and the fusion nucleus by two sperms
Fertilization of the egg and the tube cell by two sperms
rationales: Only one male gamete fertilizes the egg; the other does not fertilize that egg.
The process involves one egg and the fusion nucleus, not two eggs.
One male gamete fuses with the egg and another fuses with the fusion nucleus.
The second fusion is with the fusion nucleus, not the tube cell.

written.text: Write a short note on budding in yeast.
written.finalAnswer: Yeast reproduces asexually by budding. A small bud forms on the parent cell; its nucleus divides, and one daughter nucleus enters the bud. The bud grows and separates as a new yeast cell.

rubric.why: Identifies budding as the method and the bud's origin.
rubric.description: Name budding and state that a bud grows from the parent yeast cell.
rubric.how: State that a small outgrowth forms on the parent cell.

rubric.why: Explains how the bud becomes a new cell.
rubric.description: Explain the nuclear division and separation of the bud.
rubric.how: Mention that a daughter nucleus enters the growing bud, which separates as a new cell.

modelAnswer: Yeast reproduces asexually by budding.
A small bud forms on the parent cell.
The nucleus divides, and one daughter nucleus enters the bud.
The bud grows and separates as a new yeast cell.

written.text: Write a short note on spore formation in fungi.
written.finalAnswer: Fungi produce spores in sporangia. When mature, the sporangia release the spores. Spores are dispersed and, under favourable conditions, germinate and grow into new fungi.

rubric.why: Identifies where spores form and how they are released.
rubric.description: State that spores form in sporangia and are released when mature.
rubric.how: Name sporangia as the structures that produce or contain spores.

rubric.why: Shows how spores give rise to new fungi.
rubric.description: Explain that spores germinate in suitable conditions and form new fungi.
rubric.how: Include germination and growth into a new fungus.

modelAnswer: Fungi produce spores in sporangia.
When mature, the sporangia release the spores.
The spores are dispersed.
Under favourable conditions, a spore germinates and grows into a new fungus.

written.text: What are the advantages of spore formation in fungi and bacteria?
written.finalAnswer: Spores can be dispersed widely and can withstand unfavourable or harsh conditions. When conditions become favourable, they germinate or resume growth to form new organisms.

rubric.why: Explains how spores help organisms reach new places.
rubric.description: State that spores are small or readily dispersed to new places.
rubric.how: Mention wide dispersal, such as by air or other agents.

rubric.why: Explains how spores improve survival and allow growth later.
rubric.description: State that spores resist harsh conditions and can grow when conditions improve.
rubric.how: Mention survival in adverse conditions and later germination or growth.

modelAnswer: Spores can be dispersed widely to new places.
They can withstand harsh or unfavourable conditions.
When conditions become favourable, they germinate or resume growth to form new organisms.

written.text: Describe how vegetative propagation occurs through runners.
written.finalAnswer: A runner is a horizontal aboveground stem. It grows out from the parent plant, and roots and shoots develop at its nodes. These nodes grow into new plants, which may become independent of the parent.

rubric.why: Correctly identifies the runner and its position.
rubric.description: Describe a runner as a horizontal stem growing above the ground.
rubric.how: Include both horizontal growth and aboveground position.

rubric.why: Explains how nodes on the runner make new plants.
rubric.description: State that nodes form roots and shoots which grow into new plants.
rubric.how: Mention node development into plantlets, with separation or independence if appropriate.

modelAnswer: A runner is a horizontal aboveground stem.
It grows out from the parent plant.
Roots and shoots develop at the nodes of the runner.
These nodes grow into new plants, which may become independent of the parent.

written.text: State how potatoes reproduce through tubers.
written.finalAnswer: A potato tuber is an underground modified stem with buds called eyes. The eyes sprout and grow into shoots and roots, producing a new potato plant.

rubric.why: Identifies the tuber as the vegetative part that reproduces.
rubric.description: State that a potato tuber is an underground modified stem.
rubric.how: Name the tuber and its stem nature.

rubric.why: Explains how the buds on the tuber form a new plant.
rubric.description: Explain that eyes sprout and develop into a new plant.
rubric.how: Mention eyes or buds and the shoots or roots they produce.

modelAnswer: A potato tuber is an underground modified stem with buds called eyes.
The eyes sprout and grow into shoots and roots.
These develop into a new potato plant.

written.text: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of vegetative propagation.
written.finalAnswer: Advantages: it is a rapid method, needs only one parent, and produces plants with the same desirable characters as the parent. Disadvantages: offspring have little genetic variation, so a disease or environmental change may affect them all; diseases may also pass from parent to offspring.

rubric.why: Gives valid benefits of vegetative propagation.
rubric.description: State advantages such as speed, one parent, or preservation of desirable traits.
rubric.how: Give at least one accurate advantage.

rubric.why: Gives a valid limitation of producing genetically similar offspring.
rubric.description: State that low variation makes offspring vulnerable to shared threats or diseases.
rubric.how: Explain at least one disadvantage accurately.

modelAnswer: Advantages: vegetative propagation is rapid and requires only one parent.
It can produce many plants with the same desirable characters as the parent.
Disadvantages: the offspring have little genetic variation.
A disease or environmental change may therefore affect many of them, and diseases can pass from parent to offspring.

written.text: Name the four whorls present in a flower and also tell the components of each whorl.
written.finalAnswer: The four whorls are calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens: anther and filament), and gynoecium or carpel (stigma, style and ovary).

rubric.why: Names the four flower whorls.
rubric.description: Name calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.
rubric.how: List all four whorls.

rubric.why: Correctly identifies the components of each whorl.
rubric.description: Give sepals, petals, anther and filament, and stigma, style and ovary as the respective components.
rubric.how: Match each whorl with its constituent parts.

modelAnswer: The four whorls are calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.
Calyx consists of sepals; corolla consists of petals.
Androecium consists of stamens, each with an anther and filament.
Gynoecium (carpel) consists of stigma, style and ovary.

written.text: Briefly describe the formation of egg cell and polar nuclei within embryo sac of a flower.
written.finalAnswer: A megaspore mother cell in the ovule undergoes meiosis and forms four haploid megaspores. Usually three degenerate and the remaining megaspore undergoes three mitotic divisions, forming eight nuclei. These arrange in the embryo sac, including one egg cell and two polar nuclei in the central cell.

rubric.why: Describes the division sequence that forms the embryo-sac nuclei.
rubric.description: Explain that meiosis forms megaspores and the functional megaspore divides mitotically.
rubric.how: Include the megaspore mother cell, meiosis, and subsequent mitosis.

rubric.why: Identifies the requested cells and their arrangement.
rubric.description: State that the embryo sac contains an egg cell and two polar nuclei.
rubric.how: Name both the egg and the two polar nuclei.

modelAnswer: A megaspore mother cell in the ovule undergoes meiosis and forms four haploid megaspores.
Usually three megaspores degenerate; the remaining megaspore undergoes three mitotic divisions and forms eight nuclei.
The nuclei arrange within the embryo sac, including an egg cell and two polar nuclei in the central cell.

written.text: Differentiate between: (a) Asexual and sexual reproduction
written.finalAnswer: Asexual reproduction involves one parent and no fusion of gametes; offspring are usually genetically similar. Sexual reproduction involves male and female gametes fusing; offspring show genetic variation.

rubric.why: States the defining features of asexual reproduction.
rubric.description: Describe asexual reproduction as involving one parent without gamete fusion.
rubric.how: Mention one parent and no fusion of gametes.

rubric.why: States the defining features of sexual reproduction.
rubric.description: Describe sexual reproduction as involving gamete fusion and genetic variation.
rubric.how: Mention fusion of male and female gametes.

modelAnswer: Asexual reproduction involves one parent and no fusion of gametes; offspring are usually genetically similar.
Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of male and female gametes; offspring show genetic variation.

written.text: Differentiate between: (b) Binary fission in bacteria and amoeba
written.finalAnswer: In bacteria, the DNA replicates and the cell divides by a simple transverse division; the cell lacks a true nucleus. In Amoeba, the nucleus divides first by mitosis, followed by division of the cytoplasm, usually in any plane.

rubric.why: Distinguishes bacterial fission from division in a eukaryotic cell.
rubric.description: State that a bacterium has no true nucleus and divides after DNA replication.
rubric.how: Give the bacterial sequence or its lack of a true nucleus.

rubric.why: Describes the ordered nuclear and cytoplasmic division in Amoeba.
rubric.description: State that Amoeba's nucleus divides first, followed by cytoplasmic division.
rubric.how: Mention nuclear division followed by division of the cytoplasm.

modelAnswer: In bacteria, the DNA replicates and the cell divides by a simple transverse division; the cell has no true nucleus.
In Amoeba, the nucleus divides first by mitosis.
The cytoplasm then divides, usually in any plane.

written.text: Differentiate between: (iii) Stolon and rhizome
written.finalAnswer: A stolon is a horizontal aboveground stem; a rhizome is a horizontal underground stem.

rubric.why: Correctly identifies the position of the stolon.
rubric.description: Describe a stolon as a horizontal stem above the ground.
rubric.how: State that the stolon is aboveground.

rubric.why: Correctly identifies the position of the rhizome.
rubric.description: Describe a rhizome as a horizontal underground stem.
rubric.how: State that the rhizome is underground.

modelAnswer: A stolon is a horizontal aboveground stem.
A rhizome is a horizontal underground stem.

written.text: Differentiate between: (iv) Bulb and corm
written.finalAnswer: A bulb is a short underground stem surrounded by fleshy scale leaves; a corm is a swollen underground stem covered by dry scale leaves.

rubric.why: Describes the distinguishing structure of a bulb.
rubric.description: State that a bulb has fleshy scale leaves around a short stem.
rubric.how: Mention its fleshy leaves or scales.

rubric.why: Describes the distinguishing structure of a corm.
rubric.description: State that a corm is a swollen underground stem with dry scale leaves.
rubric.how: Mention its swollen stem and dry covering.

modelAnswer: A bulb has a short underground stem surrounded by fleshy scale leaves.
A corm is a swollen underground stem covered by dry scale leaves.

written.text: Differentiate between: (v) Cutting and grafting
written.finalAnswer: In cutting, a cut piece of a stem, root or leaf develops roots and shoots to form a new plant. In grafting, a shoot or bud of one plant (scion) is joined to the rooted stem of another plant (stock).

rubric.why: Explains how cutting produces a new plant.
rubric.description: Describe planting a cut vegetative part so it roots and grows.
rubric.how: Mention the cut piece and its development into a plant.

rubric.why: Identifies the two parts joined in grafting.
rubric.description: Explain that a scion is joined to a stock.
rubric.how: Name scion and stock and state that they are joined.

modelAnswer: In cutting, a cut piece of a stem, root or leaf develops roots and shoots to form a new plant.
In grafting, a shoot or bud of one plant, called the scion, is joined to the rooted stem of another plant, called the stock.

written.text: Differentiate between: (vi) Vegetative propagation and artificial propagation
written.finalAnswer: Vegetative propagation is the formation of new plants from vegetative parts of a plant and may occur naturally or artificially. Artificial propagation is propagation carried out by humans using methods such as cutting, grafting or layering.

rubric.why: Defines vegetative propagation by the plant parts involved.
rubric.description: State that vegetative propagation uses roots, stems or leaves and can occur naturally or artificially.
rubric.how: Mention vegetative plant parts.

rubric.why: Explains the human-directed nature and examples of artificial propagation.
rubric.description: State that humans carry out artificial propagation using methods such as cuttings or grafting.
rubric.how: Mention human involvement and an appropriate method.

modelAnswer: Vegetative propagation forms new plants from vegetative parts such as roots, stems or leaves; it may be natural or artificial.
Artificial propagation is carried out by humans using methods such as cutting, grafting or layering.

written.text: Differentiate between: (vii) Male and female gametophytes
written.finalAnswer: The male gametophyte in flowering plants is the pollen grain and produces male gametes. The female gametophyte is the embryo sac within the ovule and contains the egg cell and polar nuclei.

rubric.why: Identifies the male gametophyte and its role.
rubric.description: State that the pollen grain is the male gametophyte and produces male gametes.
rubric.how: Name pollen grain and its male function.

rubric.why: Identifies the female gametophyte and its location or contents.
rubric.description: State that the embryo sac lies in the ovule and contains the egg cell.
rubric.how: Name the embryo sac and ovule.

modelAnswer: The male gametophyte is the pollen grain, which produces male gametes.
The female gametophyte is the embryo sac within the ovule; it contains the egg cell and polar nuclei.

written.text: Differentiate between: (viii) Calyx and corolla
written.finalAnswer: The calyx is the outermost whorl of a flower and consists of sepals. The corolla is the whorl inside the calyx and consists of petals.

rubric.why: Identifies the calyx and its components or position.
rubric.description: State that the calyx consists of sepals and is the outermost whorl.
rubric.how: Name sepals or its outer position.

rubric.why: Identifies the corolla and its components or position.
rubric.description: State that the corolla consists of petals and lies inside the calyx.
rubric.how: Name petals or its position.

modelAnswer: The calyx is the outermost whorl and consists of sepals.
The corolla lies inside the calyx and consists of petals.

written.text: Differentiate between: (ix) Stamen and carpel
written.finalAnswer: The stamen is the male reproductive part of a flower and consists of anther and filament. The carpel is the female reproductive part and consists of stigma, style and ovary.

rubric.why: Identifies the stamen's reproductive role and components.
rubric.description: State that the stamen is male and has an anther and filament.
rubric.how: Name its role and parts.

rubric.why: Identifies the carpel's reproductive role and components.
rubric.description: State that the carpel is female and has stigma, style and ovary.
rubric.how: Name its role and parts.

modelAnswer: The stamen is the male reproductive part of a flower and consists of anther and filament.
The carpel is the female reproductive part and consists of stigma, style and ovary.

written.text: Explain the process of binary fission in bacteria and describe how it leads to the formation of two daughter bacteria.
written.finalAnswer: The bacterial DNA replicates. The two DNA copies attach to the cell membrane as the cell grows and elongates. The membrane and cell wall grow inward to form a septum, dividing the cell into two genetically identical daughter bacteria.

rubric.why: Replication is the first essential step before the cell can divide.
rubric.description: State that bacterial DNA replicates.
rubric.how: Show that two DNA copies are made.

rubric.why: Explains how the DNA copies become separated as the bacterium grows.
rubric.description: Describe cell growth or elongation and separation of DNA copies.
rubric.how: Mention the DNA copies moving apart as the cell elongates.

rubric.why: Identifies the division structure that separates the cell.
rubric.description: Explain that the membrane and wall constrict or form a septum.
rubric.how: Describe inward growth between the DNA copies.

rubric.why: States the outcome of binary fission.
rubric.description: State that two daughter bacteria are formed, usually genetically identical.
rubric.how: Give the number and identity of the daughter cells.

modelAnswer: The bacterial DNA replicates, producing two copies.
As the cell grows and elongates, the DNA copies move apart.
The cell membrane and wall grow inward between the copies, forming a septum.
The cell separates into two genetically identical daughter bacteria.

written.text: What do you mean by vegetative propagation? Differentiate among different plant structures modified for vegetative propagation.
written.finalAnswer: Vegetative propagation is asexual reproduction in which new plants grow from vegetative parts of a parent plant. Modified structures include runners or stolons (horizontal aboveground stems), rhizomes (horizontal underground stems), tubers (swollen underground stems with buds), bulbs (short stems with fleshy scale leaves) and corms (swollen underground stems with dry scale leaves).

rubric.why: Defines the process being asked about.
rubric.description: Define vegetative propagation as new plant formation from vegetative parts.
rubric.how: Include that it is asexual and uses a parent plant's vegetative parts.

rubric.why: Distinguishes a runner from underground structures.
rubric.description: Describe runners or stolons as horizontal aboveground stems.
rubric.how: Name the structure and its position.

rubric.why: Identifies underground stem structures and their key feature.
rubric.description: Describe rhizomes and tubers accurately.
rubric.how: Mention horizontal underground rhizomes or buds on tubers.

rubric.why: Distinguishes bulbs from corms by their structure.
rubric.description: Describe the defining features of bulbs and corms.
rubric.how: Contrast fleshy scale leaves with a swollen stem and dry scales.

rubric.why: Completes the comparison with examples of modified structures.
rubric.description: Include examples that represent the structures described.
rubric.how: Name examples such as strawberry, ginger, potato, onion or corm-producing plants.

modelAnswer: Vegetative propagation is asexual reproduction in which new plants grow from vegetative parts of a parent plant.
A runner or stolon is a horizontal aboveground stem that forms roots and shoots at its nodes; strawberry is an example.
A rhizome is a horizontal underground stem; ginger is an example.
A tuber is a swollen underground stem with buds or eyes; potato is an example.
A bulb has a short stem surrounded by fleshy scale leaves, as in onion; a corm is a swollen underground stem covered by dry scale leaves.

written.text: Describe the ways by which humans can grow new plants by using the vegetative parts of the parent plants?
written.finalAnswer: Humans can use cuttings, grafting and layering. In cutting, a piece of stem, root or leaf is planted and develops into a new plant. In grafting, a scion is joined to the stock. In layering, a branch is encouraged to form roots while attached to the parent, then is separated and planted.

rubric.why: Describes a valid human method of vegetative propagation.
rubric.description: Explain how a cutting grows into a new plant.
rubric.how: Mention a cut vegetative part and root or shoot growth.

rubric.why: Explains grafting using the correct names for its parts.
rubric.description: State that the scion is joined to the stock.
rubric.how: Name scion and stock.

rubric.why: Describes the essential feature of layering.
rubric.description: Explain that a branch forms roots while attached to its parent.
rubric.how: Mention root development before separation.

rubric.why: Completes the method description with new-plant formation and suitable methods.
rubric.description: State how the rooted part is separated or name the propagation methods.
rubric.how: Include the new plant outcome and method names.

modelAnswer: Humans can use methods such as cutting, grafting and layering.
In cutting, a piece of stem, root or leaf is planted; it develops roots and shoots and forms a new plant.
In grafting, a shoot or bud called the scion is joined to the rooted part called the stock.
In layering, a branch is encouraged to form roots while still attached to the parent; it is then separated and planted.

written.text: Define sporophyte and gametophyte. State their roles in the life cycle of plants.
written.finalAnswer: The sporophyte is the diploid (2n) generation that produces haploid spores by meiosis. The gametophyte is the haploid (n) generation that develops from a spore and produces gametes by mitosis. Fertilization of gametes forms a diploid zygote that develops into the sporophyte.

rubric.why: Defines the sporophyte by its chromosome number.
rubric.description: State that the sporophyte is the diploid plant generation.
rubric.how: Include diploid or 2n.

rubric.why: States the sporophyte's role in producing spores.
rubric.description: Explain that the sporophyte produces spores by meiosis.
rubric.how: Connect spore formation with meiosis.

rubric.why: Defines the gametophyte and its gamete-producing role.
rubric.description: State that the haploid gametophyte produces gametes by mitosis.
rubric.how: Include haploid or n and gamete production.

rubric.why: Explains how the two generations follow one another.
rubric.description: Explain that fertilization forms a diploid zygote that develops into the sporophyte.
rubric.how: Link gamete fusion to the next sporophyte generation.

modelAnswer: The sporophyte is the diploid (2n) generation of a plant.
It produces haploid spores by meiosis.
The gametophyte is the haploid (n) generation, which develops from a spore.
It produces gametes by mitosis; fertilization forms a diploid zygote that develops into the sporophyte.

written.text: Explain the lifecycle of flowering plants, focusing on the alternation between the gametophyte and sporophyte generations.
written.finalAnswer: The dominant flowering-plant sporophyte (2n) forms flowers. Meiosis produces haploid spores: microspores develop into pollen grains, the male gametophytes, and a megaspore develops into the embryo sac, the female gametophyte. The gametophytes form male and female gametes. After pollination, a pollen tube carries male gametes to the embryo sac. One male gamete fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote; the other fuses with the polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm. The zygote develops into an embryo, and the ovule becomes a seed that germinates into a new sporophyte.

rubric.why: Begins the cycle with the correct dominant generation.
rubric.description: State that the flowering plant is the diploid sporophyte.
rubric.how: Identify the adult plant as 2n.

rubric.why: Explains how spores and gametophytes arise.
rubric.description: Describe meiosis and development of pollen and embryo sac.
rubric.how: Connect spores with male and female gametophyte formation.

rubric.why: Explains how male gametes reach the female gametophyte.
rubric.description: Describe pollen germination and pollen-tube transport.
rubric.how: Mention the pollen tube reaching the embryo sac.

rubric.why: Includes the two fertilization events in flowering plants.
rubric.description: Explain the zygote and endosperm-forming fusions.
rubric.how: State both the egg fusion and polar-nuclei fusion.

rubric.why: Completes the alternation by linking seed growth to the next plant.
rubric.description: Explain seed/embryo development and the new sporophyte.
rubric.how: End with germination into a new flowering plant.

modelAnswer: The adult flowering plant is the diploid sporophyte (2n), which produces flowers.
Meiosis forms haploid spores. Microspores develop into pollen grains, the male gametophytes; a megaspore develops into the embryo sac, the female gametophyte.
The male gametophyte forms male gametes, and the female gametophyte contains the egg cell and polar nuclei.
After pollination, a pollen tube grows to the embryo sac and carries the male gametes.
One male gamete fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote; the other fuses with the polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm. This is double fertilization.
The zygote develops into an embryo; the ovule becomes a seed, which germinates to form a new sporophyte.

written.text: Describe how the female gametophyte (embryo sac) develops within the ovule of a flower.
written.finalAnswer: A diploid megaspore mother cell in the ovule undergoes meiosis to form four haploid megaspores. Three usually degenerate. The remaining functional megaspore undergoes three mitotic divisions, forming eight haploid nuclei. These arrange into a seven-celled embryo sac: an egg cell and two synergids at one end, three antipodal cells at the other end, and a central cell containing two polar nuclei.

rubric.why: Identifies the starting cell and its location and division.
rubric.description: State that a megaspore mother cell in the ovule undergoes meiosis.
rubric.how: Name the cell, location and meiosis.

rubric.why: Explains how one functional megaspore remains.
rubric.description: State that meiosis forms four megaspores and usually three degenerate.
rubric.how: Include the number and the fate of the megaspores.

rubric.why: Explains the nuclear divisions that form the embryo sac.
rubric.description: State that the remaining megaspore divides three times to form eight nuclei.
rubric.how: Include three divisions and eight nuclei.

rubric.why: Shows the final arrangement of embryo-sac cells and nuclei.
rubric.description: Describe the egg apparatus, antipodals and central polar nuclei.
rubric.how: Name the main cells and the two polar nuclei.

modelAnswer: A diploid megaspore mother cell in the ovule undergoes meiosis and forms four haploid megaspores.
Usually three megaspores degenerate, leaving one functional megaspore.
The functional megaspore undergoes three mitotic divisions, forming eight haploid nuclei.
The nuclei arrange into a seven-celled embryo sac: an egg cell and two synergids at one end, three antipodal cells at the other end, and a central cell with two polar nuclei.

written.text: Why are spores considered an adaptation for survival in harsh environmental conditions?
written.finalAnswer: Many spores have protective coverings and can remain dormant, allowing them to resist harsh conditions such as dryness or extreme temperatures. They can be dispersed and germinate when conditions become favourable.

rubric.why: Identifies the protective feature that helps spores survive.
rubric.description: State that spores have a protective covering or resistant wall.
rubric.how: Name a protective spore feature.

rubric.why: Explains survival while conditions are unsuitable.
rubric.description: State that spores can remain dormant and withstand adverse conditions.
rubric.how: Give dormancy or an example of a harsh condition.

rubric.why: Explains how spores can reach other environments.
rubric.description: State that spores can be dispersed.
rubric.how: Mention movement to new places.

rubric.why: Explains when the spores resume growth.
rubric.description: State that spores germinate when conditions become favourable.
rubric.how: Include the return to growth in suitable conditions.

modelAnswer: Many spores have protective coverings and can remain dormant.
This helps them resist harsh conditions such as dryness or extreme temperatures.
Spores can also be dispersed to new places.
When conditions become favourable, they germinate and grow.

written.text: How do asexual and sexual reproduction contribute differently to genetic diversity of plant populations?
written.finalAnswer: Asexual reproduction usually produces genetically similar offspring from one parent, so it creates little genetic variation. Sexual reproduction combines genetic material from gametes, producing varied offspring and increasing genetic diversity in the population.

rubric.why: Identifies the basic nature of asexual reproduction.
rubric.description: State that asexual reproduction involves one parent and no gamete fusion.
rubric.how: Mention one parent or absence of gamete fusion.

rubric.why: Explains the effect of asexual reproduction on diversity.
rubric.description: State that asexual offspring are usually alike and add little variation.
rubric.how: Connect asexual reproduction with low variation.

rubric.why: Identifies the source of new combinations in sexual reproduction.
rubric.description: State that sexual reproduction involves fusion of gametes.
rubric.how: Mention the combination of genetic material.

rubric.why: States the effect of sexual reproduction on the population.
rubric.description: Explain that sexual reproduction generates varied offspring and greater diversity.
rubric.how: Link gamete combination to variation.

modelAnswer: Asexual reproduction involves one parent and usually produces genetically similar offspring.
It therefore creates little genetic variation in the population.
Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of gametes and combines genetic material.
It produces varied offspring and increases genetic diversity in the plant population.

written.text: How does the pollen tube facilitate the process of fertilization in flowering plants?
written.finalAnswer: After a pollen grain lands on a compatible stigma, it germinates and forms a pollen tube. The tube grows down the style into the ovary and enters an ovule, carrying the male gametes to the embryo sac. The male gametes can then fuse with the egg and the fusion nucleus in double fertilization.

rubric.why: Identifies where pollen germinates to begin tube growth.
rubric.description: State that a pollen grain lands on a compatible stigma and germinates.
rubric.how: Name the stigma and pollen germination.

rubric.why: Explains the tube's route through the flower.
rubric.description: Describe the tube growing down the style towards the ovary.
rubric.how: Mention the style and ovary.

rubric.why: Explains the tube's transport role.
rubric.description: State that the tube reaches the ovule and carries male gametes to the embryo sac.
rubric.how: Name the gametes and their destination.

rubric.why: Connects delivery of gametes to the fertilization events.
rubric.description: State that the male gametes fuse with the egg and fusion nucleus.
rubric.how: Mention the two fusions.

modelAnswer: A pollen grain lands on a compatible stigma and germinates.
It forms a pollen tube that grows down the style towards the ovary and enters an ovule.
The pollen tube carries the male gametes to the embryo sac.
There, one male gamete fuses with the egg and the other with the fusion nucleus; this is double fertilization.

examTips: Short questions commonly ask for a definition, a sequence, a function, or a difference between two structures. Use the exact textbook terms such as runner, rhizome, pollen grain and embryo sac.
For a process question, earn marks by writing the steps in order. In binary fission, show DNA replication, cell elongation, formation of a septum and two daughter bacteria.
For comparisons, use paired points so the examiner can clearly see the difference between the two terms.
Long questions on the flower life cycle and embryo-sac development need the sequence and the correct ploidy terms: haploid (n), diploid (2n) and triploid (3n).
For a flower diagram question, label each pointer neatly and use a straight line that touches the structure being named. Common labels include stigma, style, ovary, anther, filament, petal and sepal.

hints: First identify the horizontal stem as aboveground or underground.
Describe where roots and shoots form and name the example plant.
yourTurn.question: Describe how vegetative propagation occurs through runners.
solution: A runner is a horizontal aboveground stem.
It grows out from the parent plant.
Roots and shoots develop at the runner's nodes.
The rooted nodes grow into new plants, as in strawberry.
yourTurn.answer: Roots and shoots form at nodes of a horizontal aboveground runner and grow into new plants, as in strawberry.

hints: Start with the megaspore mother cell in the ovule.
Track meiosis, degeneration, mitosis and the final egg/polar nuclei.
yourTurn.question: Briefly describe the formation of egg cell and polar nuclei within embryo sac of a flower.
solution: The megaspore mother cell in the ovule undergoes meiosis to form four haploid megaspores.
The remaining megaspore undergoes three mitotic divisions, forming eight nuclei.
These arrange in the embryo sac, including an egg cell and two polar nuclei in the central cell.
yourTurn.answer: Meiosis forms four megaspores; one remains and divides three times to form eight nuclei, including the egg cell and two polar nuclei.

steps.why: The starting cell must copy its genetic material before it can divide.
steps.text: The bacterial DNA replicates, producing two copies.

steps.why: Cell growth separates the copies so each daughter cell can receive DNA.
steps.text: As the cell grows and elongates, the DNA copies move apart.

steps.why: The inward-growing cell boundary makes the division between the two DNA copies.
steps.text: The cell membrane and wall grow inward between the copies, forming a septum.

steps.why: This is the final outcome of binary fission.
steps.text: The cell separates into two genetically identical daughter bacteria.

example.question: Explain the process of binary fission in bacteria and describe how it leads to the formation of two daughter bacteria.
example.answer: Bacterial DNA replicates; the cell elongates; a septum forms between the DNA copies; the cell divides into two genetically identical daughter bacteria.

explain.title: Asexual reproduction
explain.body: Asexual reproduction needs one parent and does not involve the fusion of gametes. Binary fission in bacteria, budding in yeast, and spore formation in fungi are examples. The offspring are usually genetically similar to the parent.

explain.title: Spores and survival
explain.body: Fungi produce spores that can be dispersed and can germinate in suitable conditions. Some bacteria form thick-walled endospores in harsh conditions. Protective spores can remain dormant until conditions become favourable.

explain.title: Vegetative propagation
explain.body: New plants can grow from vegetative parts such as stems, roots or leaves. Runners and stolons grow above the ground; rhizomes, tubers, bulbs and corms are underground structures. People can also use methods such as cuttings, grafting and layering.

explain.title: Flower structure and gametophytes
explain.body: The four flower whorls are calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens) and gynoecium or carpel (stigma, style and ovary). The pollen grain is the male gametophyte; the embryo sac inside the ovule is the female gametophyte.

explain.title: Fertilization and plant generations
explain.body: A pollen grain germinates on the stigma and forms a pollen tube that carries male gametes to the embryo sac. One male gamete fuses with the egg and the other with the fusion nucleus: this is double fertilization. The embryo develops in the seed, and the seed grows into a new sporophyte plant.

mistakes: Do not call a rhizome an aboveground stem: it is underground; a runner or stolon is aboveground.
Do not confuse the male and female gametophytes: pollen grain is male, and the embryo sac is female.
Do not say that the endosperm is diploid: it is triploid (3n) in flowering plants.
In double fertilization, one male gamete fuses with the egg, while the other fuses with the fusion nucleus; the egg is not fertilized by two male gametes.
When describing spore formation, distinguish survival in harsh conditions from germination, which occurs in suitable conditions.
For binary fission, do not omit DNA replication or the formation of two daughter bacteria.
